implementation_notes: The JDK documents BlockingQueue as designed primarily for producer-consumer queues: put(e) blocks while full, take() blocks while empty, and offer(e, timeout, unit)/poll(timeout, unit) give bounded waits, so the full/empty policy is explicit at each call site. ArrayBlockingQueue is the bounded array form (with an optional fairness flag), LinkedBlockingQueue is bounded only when a capacity is given, and SynchronousQueue is the zero-capacity rendezvous. The interface is thread-safe for multiple producers and consumers but has no close operation, so the documented end-of-stream tactic is a poison object that consumers recognize; the hand-written synchronized/wait/notify buffer is unnecessary.
code_sketch:
BlockingQueue<Job> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1024);

queue.put(job);                  // producer: blocks while full

Job job = queue.take();          // consumer: blocks while empty
if (job == POISON) return;       // end-of-stream sentinel
pitfalls: new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() without a capacity is unbounded - the decoupling silently becomes memory growth.
put/take throw InterruptedException and clear the interrupt status; swallowing it breaks cancellation, so propagate it or restore the flag and exit.
There is no close: shutdown needs one poison pill per consumer (or a drained-plus-interrupted protocol), and blocked threads must be released deliberately.
Doing slow work while holding a queue-related lock - or calling into another blocking queue from inside a consumer - couples unrelated stalls and invites deadlock.

variants.name: Virtual-thread consumers over a BlockingQueue (Java 21)
variants.implementation_notes: Java 21 virtual threads change the economics, not the API: a virtual thread blocked in BlockingQueue.take() unmounts from its carrier (JEP 444 names that call explicitly), so hundreds of thousands of cheap consumer threads are possible and the 'one platform thread per consumer' capacity problem disappears. The realization is a bounded BlockingQueue plus one virtual thread per consumer, with the same poison-pill or shutdown protocol; JEP 444 also warns to never pool virtual threads - the queue bound limits work in flight, not the thread count. Avoid blocking while inside synchronized so the carrier is not pinned.
pitfalls: Pooling virtual threads defeats their purpose; one virtual thread per consumer is the intended shape.
A virtual thread blocked inside a synchronized block is pinned to its carrier; guard queue-adjacent critical sections with ReentrantLock instead (JEP 444).
Unbounded consumer fan-out without a queue bound turns the queue into the memory bottleneck.
